transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, hello, Dr. Smith. It's lovely to meet you, too. I suppose I should just start from the beginning, though it's a bit hard to pin down exactly when it all started feeling so... relentless. But really, what brings me in today is that for the past year or so, I just feel like I'm always on the go. I mean, I'm 87 years old, for heaven's sake! You'd think I'd be ready to sit in a rocking chair and knit, but no. I'm always puttering around the house. If I'm not fixing that wobbly leg on the side table in the hallway, I'm rearranging the pantry so the canned goods are alphabetical, or I'm out in the garden pulling weeds that probably don't even need pulling yet. And it doesn't stop there. The church needed someone to organize the bake sale, and before I knew it, my hand was up. Then the neighborhood watch needed a secretary, and I volunteered for that, too. It's just one more thing after another, and I just... I have such a hard time just sitting down and being still. Even when I try to watch a television program, my hands are moving, or my foot is tapping, or I'm thinking about the dust on the mantelpiece. It's just constant activity, from the moment I wake up until I finally exhaust myself enough to sleep.
Have you noticed any changes in your memory or your ability to handle tasks that you used to find easy to manage?

Oh, goodness, no. No, nothing like that. My memory is—well, knock on wood—it's still sharp as a tack. I mean, you'd think at 87 I might start misplacing my reading glasses or forgetting why I walked into a room, but no, I remember absolutely everything. 

Just last week, when I was organizing that church bake sale I mentioned, I remembered exactly who brought those awful store-bought cookies three years ago. It was Martha, bless her heart, but I made sure to put her on paper plate duty this time instead of baking. And as for handling things... well, I still handle all my own bills, I balance my checkbook down to the very last penny every single Friday morning right after my breakfast tea, and I haven't lost my touch with any of that. I even do my own taxes! 

The problem really isn't that I can't manage my tasks, Doctor, it's that I manage them perfectly well and then I immediately go looking for six more things to do! I just keep adding to the pile. But no, no confusion, no forgetting things, no trouble figuring out how to do what I've always done. I can still recite a poem I learned in my sophomore year of college, if you can believe it. "Whose woods these are I think I know..." well, I won't recite the whole thing for you right now, but you get the idea. My mind is perfectly clear, thank heavens. It just... it just absolutely refuses to take a break.

When you are keeping yourself this busy, are you doing it because you are feeling worried or anxious about something, or is it more that you simply feel like you have a surplus of energy and a strong desire to stay active?

Oh, that’s a very interesting question, Doctor. You know, my daughter Susan asked me something quite similar just last Thanksgiving when I was up at dawn making three different kinds of stuffing—because Arthur, my late husband, always liked the oyster stuffing, but the grandchildren won't touch anything that isn't plain sage and onion, and then there's my son-in-law who insists on cornbread. Anyway, Susan came into the kitchen, rubbing her eyes, and said, "Mom, are you worried about something? Why are you frantic?" And I told her then exactly what I’ll tell you now: I am not frantic, and I am certainly not worried! 

I mean, I worry about the normal things, of course. I worry if the mailman is staying hydrated in the summer heat, and I worry about whether the tomatoes will get enough sun this year because that big oak tree in the neighbor's yard just keeps growing and blocking the light, but I don't have that... that heavy, nervous feeling in my chest. It’s not dread or anxiety pushing me out of bed. It really is just this absolute surplus of energy, exactly like you said! 

It’s like I have a little motor humming inside me from the minute I open my eyes. I’ll wake up, usually around 5:30 or 6:00, and the moment my feet hit the floor, I just feel this overwhelming urge to do something. If I try to just sit and drink my morning tea, I start noticing that the baseboards need dusting, or I think about how the linen closet hasn't been properly sorted by color and season since last October. And I just can't sit there! I have to get up and tackle it. So no, it's not anxiety at all, it's just... I just have all this get-up-and-go, and at 87, I suppose it just has nowhere proper to go, so it ends up directed at the pantry shelves and the church bake sales!

Do you ever experience periods, perhaps lasting a few days or longer, where you feel the complete opposite of this—where you feel very low, lose interest in things you usually enjoy, or simply lack the energy to get out of bed?

Oh, heavens no. No, no, no. I really can't say I've ever felt like that. A few days of not wanting to get out of bed? Why, if I stayed in bed for a whole day, I think my neighbors would call the police to do a wellness check! No, I just don't have those low periods you're talking about. I've never been one to mope or lose interest in things. 

Even when Arthur passed—and oh, that was a terribly sad time, of course, we were married for fifty-two years, you know—but even then, I didn't lose my energy or stay in bed. I threw myself into organizing his memorial, and I made sure every single person who sent a casserole got a hand-written thank you note within the week. I must have written over a hundred notes! I used that lovely ivory stationery with the embossed edges that I bought at a little boutique downtown before it closed... oh, it's been a bank for a decade now, I suppose. 

But anyway, no, I don't get depressed or lethargic. I don't lose interest in my garden or my baking or my committees. If anything, I wish I could lose just a tiny bit of interest, just for an afternoon, so I could sit on the porch and read a book without feeling like I need to get up and sweep the porch steps! But no, doctor, I don't have those low, empty days at all. My engine just keeps running on high, day in and day out. I honestly can't remember the last time I felt too tired to get up and face the day. It's always just... go, go, go.
Do you often feel that your capabilities or talents are significantly superior to those of the people around you?

Oh, goodness, no! No, I wouldn't say that at all. I certainly don't think I'm better than anyone else, or that I have some sort of grand talent that other people don't have. I mean, yes, I'm very organized, and yes, I know how to run a proper bake sale—which, frankly, is a dying art, if you ask me, because half the women these days just want to buy a tray of brownies from the supermarket bakery and call it a day, which completely defeats the purpose of a *bake* sale, doesn't it? But that's just a matter of having standards and putting in the effort, not because I'm some sort of genius or superior being! 

I really just think I have a lot of practical experience. When you've lived 87 years, you pick up a few things, like knowing that you always need twice as much change in the cash box as you think you will, and that you should never put the chocolate items in the direct sun if the sale is outdoors. But I don't walk around thinking I'm smarter or more capable than my friends or the other ladies at the church. In fact, Martha—the one with the store-bought cookies I mentioned earlier—she is an absolutely brilliant seamstress. She made the most beautiful christening gown for her granddaughter last spring, with all this intricate smocking and tiny little pearl buttons. I could never do that! My hands just won't stay still long enough for that kind of fine, detailed needlework. I'd be up and pacing around the room before I finished the first row of stitches. 

So, no, I definitely don't feel superior. I just feel... well, I just feel busy! I know what I'm good at, like keeping things moving and getting things done, but I certainly appreciate what other people can do, too. I just wish I could get everyone else to move a little faster sometimes, that's all! But no, no grand ideas about being better than anyone else. Just... very, very energetic.
How many hours of sleep do you typically get at night, and do you find that you wake up feeling fully refreshed even after only a few hours of rest?

Oh, goodness, no! If I only got a few hours of sleep, I would be absolutely useless the next day. I know I told you earlier that I wake up at 5:30 or 6:00 with that little motor running, but you have to understand, I am in bed very early to make up for it. 

I usually head up the stairs right after Jeopardy—well, sometimes I stay up for Wheel of Fortune if it's a tournament week or if they have a particularly good puzzle board, but usually, by 8:30, I'm in the bathroom washing my face and putting on my night cream. It's this wonderful thick cream with rosehip oil that my daughter Susan orders for me from some fancy store online, because they stopped carrying it at the pharmacy in town. Anyway, by the time I read a chapter or two of my book, I'm asleep by 9:30 or 10:00 at the absolute latest. So if you do the math, I'm getting a solid seven and a half to eight hours every single night. 

I definitely don't have that thing where you can just sleep for three hours and feel fine. Oh heavens, no. There was one time, it must have been about three years ago in the dead of winter, when the Johnsons down the street had a water main burst in the middle of the night. The fire trucks came with their sirens blaring and those awful flashing lights right through my bedroom window at 2:00 AM. Well, I was up for the rest of the night, just tossing and turning and worrying about their carpets. And let me tell you, the next day I felt like I had been run over by a tractor! I couldn't even focus enough to bake my usual Tuesday morning bran muffins. I just sat at the kitchen island staring at the flour canister, completely drained. 

So I absolutely need my full night's rest. It's just that once I *have* had my seven or eight hours, the moment my eyes open, that energy is back and I simply have to get moving. But I certainly couldn't keep up my schedule on just a few hours of sleep. My body would just go on strike!
